content.summary_of_the_paper:
The manuscript introduces a way to jointly learn 3D object detection as well as a per-object dense matchable feature map. These per-object feature maps are leveraged to perform object-level bundle adjustment to optimize the 3D object pose over the full tracklet. 

This object BA demonstrably improves object pose estimates over the initialization of object poses from the object detector and tracker (via 3D Kalman filter). 

Notably this approach can handle dynamic objects and shows significantly improved performance over related work. Ablations show that the key to this improvement is the ability to optimize the object poses from the learned feature maps.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
It is great to see this work bring together the two worlds of 3D object detection and Bundle Adjustment in this system and see it improve performance.  I also agree strongly with the need for multi-view/video 3D Object detection works to handle dynamic objects and this work addresses this convincingly.

Another way of thinking about the classification of systems in Fig 1 is that there are early fusion methods (fuse multi-view information into a feature volume or BEV grid first then detect objects) and late fusion methods (detect objects first, then associate and track). The key problem that feature-based methods have is how to handle dynamics as stated by the authors. The key problem that late fusion methods (like the proposed one) have is to associate per-frame detections and to handle miss-associations. 
The object detection association problem was not really evaluated (and not a key contribution of this work). It would still be interesting to comment on it in the paper. For example I wonder if the RANSAC-based feature association allows identifying and dropping incorrect associations made by the object tracking system?

The evaluation is strong and done well. It supports the claims that the feature-metric object pose estimation for each tracklet does improve performance (over just 3D Kalman filter) and that this leads to state of the art performance that significantly outperforms related work. 

The main weakness of the work to my mind is that the explanation of the approach is not very clear. In particular the core section 4.2 is hard to follow because it seems there are concepts thrown together that are needed during training and during inference. 
As far as I can tell up to Eq 8 the manuscript talks about training time, then it switches to talking about how to optimize the pose during inference till Eq 11 and then it switches back to talking about how to supervise the correspondence map during training.
Among the things that are unclear to me (after putting significant effort into trying to understand the section):
- "Given the 3D points P_k on the object" does not literally mean we are given the points - they are part of the BA. Need to clarify the language. What is given what is optimized?
- After Eq 10 a network H_\theta is referenced that I could not find anywhere else in the paper. This means it is unclear how the prediction happens from one frame to the other? I was assuming the correspondence map might be used?  It also seems like RANSAC might be used (Sec 4.3). This is very unclear. 
- "z_i is the groundtruth depth" where does the groundtruth depth come from? As far as I can tell this method aims to not use any depth sensor? Does it come from some other part of the network that is not shown? MonoFlex seems to regress some depth values? Is that it? If so this needs to be shown in the diagrams and clarified in the text.
- In Eq 12 the groundtruth correspondent 2d points are referenced but I dont understand where those would come from since we dont really have the P_k points on the objects? We only have the groundtruth pose. 

I strongly advice to split out the training and inference parts more clearly.  What is used during training what during inference and why?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The manuscript is quite clear except for the approach section 4 (see weaknesses).
Similarly the quality of the work is high except for the approach section. There are some good illustrative figures that help understand the problem but the structure of Section 4 makes it hard to follow the approach.
The work seems original. It draws on two fields of 3D perception that are not commonly brought together and shows convincingly how to leverage both to significantly improve 3D object detection and tracking.

Because of the lack of clarity in the approach section 4 I could not reproduce the work purely based on the paper. However the authors promise to release the code which should help.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the work would be a great contribution to the 3D detection and tracking community. However, since it is hard to follow the approach section, I cannot recommend accept without the manuscript being revised or clarified by the authors.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present their work on 3D object detection using correspondences in video. They do this in two stages - the first stage is a monocular 3D object detection (CenterNet) and second stage is a proposed object centric temporal correspondence module (OTCL).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- The method is well thought out 
- The results show improvement on SOTA


Weaknesses: 

- The paper lacks details significantly.
- The motivation for the work including evaluation is poorly justified. E.g., Why monoflex was chosen as baseline
- Ablation study needs more details. Not entirely clear what is being compared with the baseline.
- Needs evaluation with more datasets e.g., KITTI, nuScenes etc.,
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is unclear in many places. The quality of the writing needs to be improved to provide clarity. (E.g. section 2) 
- The code needs to be released. 
- I would strongly suggest to attach supplemental material with additional details on how the training was performed, and pictures of inference.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper tackles an interesting topic of 3D object detection. However the quality of the submission needs to be improved as it is lacking significant details and the novelty of the work or the claims are unclear.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the problem of modeling object motion in monocular 3D object detection from videos. It comprehensively revisits previous works with their weaknesses and proposes an object-centric bundle adjustment method to globally optimize the object pose estimation and feature correspondence learning jointly. This two-stage framework first detects objects and extracts RoIs at first, and uses a feature metric bundle adjustment loss to learn a feature correspondence network during training as well as inference object poses during inference. It achieves a new SoTA on the Waymo dataset with marginal computational overheads.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The analysis of previous works is comprehensive and insightful, with an in-depth discussion of their weaknesses.
- The main idea is novel and suitable to tackle the object motion modeling problem.
- Illustrations and the overall presentation are clear.
- Experiments show the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method with SoTA results.
- Some empirical studies/discussions are interesting and enlightening, such as the comparison of traditional ORB features and the learned dense features, and the qualitative results in Fig. 4.

Weaknesses:
- (Main) Waymo experimental results are out-of-date, somehow unfair with incorrect results. First, Waymo has proposed LET-AP metrics for camera-only 3D detection recently and set up an official benchmark for this task, but this paper still uses the old strict metrics, which is not suitable for this task and misses more state-of-the-art entries (BEVFormer++, MV-FCOS3D++, DETR4D, etc.). Second, the evaluation of PCT, MonoJSG, and some others use the ground truths from the whole scene (instead of only the front view) and thus shows much lower performance than others. They also show better performance on KITTI and nuScenes, where many methods try their best to achieve a competitive result and will be more convincing to be compared.
Therefore, I recommend the authors first supplement the benchmark with new results under the LET-AP metrics and would better add results on KITTI and nuScenes.
- Another problem is that some description in the methodology is unclear, such as:
1. What are the "3D points on the objects"? Are they derived by using LiDAR projections during inference or approximated by the ground truth 3D bounding boxes (like 8 corner points of them)?
2. What is the ground-truth depth in Eqn. (10)? It is a problem closely related to question 1. Is it derived by object annotations or LiDAR projections?
3. Some notations are confusing. For example, T represents the camera pose in the object reference frame in Eqn. (7) and changes to the ground-truth pose of objects in Eqn. (10).
4. How does the network train the 2D bounding box head? Using the tightly annotated 2D boxes or the minimal outer 2D boxes of projected 3D boxes?
5. The post-processing is a little hand-crafted such that the details are hard to grasp with the description in Sec. 4.3. It may need more introduction in the supplemental.
- Minor comments:
1. Why not combine object-centric optimization with stereo matching for the background regions? From my understanding, these two components do not have conflicts with each other?
2. line 3 in Sec. 2.1: there is a miss cite after "Message passing network".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Overall clear but has confusing points in the methodology part.

Quality: Decent but need improvement in terms of more convincing experimental results.

Novelty: Overall good.

Reproducibility: Fair. It is hard to reproduce it with only the implementation details of the paper because there are some hand-crafted engineering details. Nevertheless, the author promises the code release in the abstract, which may make it easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes an effective and efficient method to deal with object motion modeling in monocular 3D detection from videos. The bundle adjustment optimization is used for learning dense feature correspondence with object pose ground truths and inferencing object poses with the trained correspondence network. The ablation studies demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, but the experiments have some problems in terms of correctness and fairness. There are also minor points required to be clarified for the methodology part. I would recommend borderline rejection and might consider raising the grade if the author can address some of my concerns in the discussion phase.

content.title: Video-based 3D Object Detection with Learnable Object-Centric Global Optimization
content.abstract: We study utilizing long-term temporal visual correspondence-based optimization for video-based 3D object detection in this work. Visual correspondence refers to one-to-one mappings for pixels across multiple images. Correspondence-based optimization is the cornerstone for 3D scene reconstruction but is less studied in 3D object detection, for that moving objects violate multi-view geometry constraints and are treated as outliers during scene reconstruction. We resolve this issue by treating objects as first-class citizens during correspondence-based optimization. In this work, we propose BA-Det, an end-to-end optimizable object detector with object-centric temporal correspondence learning and object-centric featuremetric bundle adjustment. Empirically, we verify the effectiveness and efficiency of BA-Det for multiple baseline 3D detectors under various setups. Our BA-Det achieves SOTA performance on the large-scale Waymo Open Dataset (WOD) with only marginal computation cost.  Codes will be released soon.
